title: Assigning Isn't Teaching
author: Rod Naquin
summary: Rod Naquin, an English teacher and mentor, begins with a student teacher whose Great Gatsby task fell apart because she had never written an answer to her own question. He uses the moment to argue that much of what looks like a classroom management problem is really a gap between assigning and teaching. He draws on Dolores Durkin's 1970s observations of comprehension instruction, which found teachers mentioning a skill, assigning practice and checking answers rather than teaching it, and on Barak Rosenshine's finding that the most effective teachers spent about twice as long explaining, modeling and guiding practice. The TNTP Opportunity Myth study supplies the scale: students were busy and earned good grades yet showed grade-level mastery only 17 percent of the time. Naquin warns that the fix is not an easier task but a bridge to the demanding one. He closes with a coaching routine, Take the Student's Seat, in which mentor and teacher complete the task cold before it is assigned and compare answers.
points: Durkin's classroom observations found teachers mentioning a skill, assigning practice and checking it, so students who already knew how to do the work thrived and everyone else guessed.

Rosenshine found the most effective teachers spent about 23 minutes of a 40-minute period explaining and modeling against about 11 for the least effective, which shifts error correction away from desk-to-desk repair.
The Opportunity Myth data show students busy 88 percent of the time and meeting assignment demands 71 percent of the time, yet reaching grade-level mastery only 17 percent of the time.
Easier assignments are the wrong remedy; the right one is keeping the demanding task and building the modeling and guided practice students need to reach it.
The Take the Student's Seat coaching routine has mentor and teacher answer the task cold, then examine where they hesitated, what students would need to know, and what must be shown first.
quotes: In the late 1970s, a reading researcher named Dolores Durkin went looking for comprehension instruction in upper elementary classrooms. Her team watched close to 75 hours of reading lessons and found only about 20 minutes of actually teaching students how to understand what they read.
Durkin gave the pattern a name that still stings: mentioning. She defined it as “saying just enough about a topic” for students to complete an exercise on it.
The students who already know how thrive. Everyone else guesses, and from the front of the room, guessing looks a lot like misbehavior.
As Rosenshine put it, “practice can be a disaster if students are practicing errors.” Much of what we call a management problem is an instruction problem showing up late.

Students were working on class activities 88 percent of the time. They met the demands of their assignments 71 percent of the time, and more than half brought home As and Bs. Yet they showed mastery of grade-level standards only 17 percent of the time.
That gap is the trap. A quiet room full of students filling in a handout looks like success, and the gradebook agrees.
Teaching means keeping the demanding task and building the bridge students need to reach it.
Before a task goes in front of students, the mentor or leader says, “Let’s both do this one first, cold, the way a student would. Then show me your answer.
